exercises.explain: helfen takes the dative — one of a small group of verbs where German and English disagree about the case.
The person receiving is dative, the thing given is accusative: ich gebe dir das Buch.
sehen takes the accusative: ihn. „ihm“ would be the dative.
danken takes the dative — and uns is the same in both cases, which is why it feels easy.
gehören takes the dative: ihr.
The recipient is dative: ihm. Compare „ich sehe ihn“, where he is the object seen.
gefallen takes the dative, and the *picture* is the subject: it pleases you.
anrufen takes the accusative — and uns again looks identical.
euch is both accusative and dative; here it is the dative recipient.
A short list worth learning whole: helfen, danken, gehören, gefallen, antworten, folgen, passen, schmecken.
Movement into somewhere: in + das = ins Kino.
Position, so dative: an + dem = am. „an dem“ is not wrong, just unusual.
die Arbeit is feminine: zu + der = zur.
von + dem = vom. Coming *from*, so von; going *to* would be zum.
bei + dem = beim.
der Supermarkt is masculine: zu + dem = zum.
sich freuen auf takes the accusative: auf + das = aufs.
There is **no** contraction for in + der. This is the trap: im is in + dem, not in + der.
für + das = fürs, and für always takes the accusative.
im (in dem), ins (in das), zur (zu der), zum (zu dem), am, ans, beim, vom — but never in + der.
sehr is the strongest of the everyday intensifiers.
gar only appears with a negation: gar nicht, gar kein. On its own it means nothing.

exercises.prompt: Das Essen war ___ gut. (besser als okay, nicht super)
exercises.explain: ziemlich sits in the middle: quite, fairly.
gar kein = none at all.
Fairly cold — noticeable, not extreme.

exercises.prompt: Sie spricht ___ gut Deutsch. (freundlich, aber nicht perfekt)
exercises.explain: Unstressed „ganz gut“ softens rather than strengthens — it means „pretty good“, not „completely good“.
The strongest negation available at this level.
sehr > ziemlich > ganz, with ganz the weakest when it is unstressed.
The commonest misunderstanding at A2: it sounds like praise and is only half of one.
gar nicht, gar kein, gar nichts — never on its own.
Professions after sein or werden take no article. „ein Lehrer“ is possible but stresses a role rather than stating a job.
After als the noun stands bare.
Hunger, Durst, Angst and Zeit are used without an article.
Cities and most countries take no article at all.
Materials take no article: aus Gold, aus Holz, aus Plastik.
Languages take no article after lernen or sprechen.
Angst haben vor + Dativ, with no article on Angst.
A substance in general takes no article. „einen Kaffee“ would mean one cup.

options: bei Berufen, Nationalitäten, Materialien und Sprachen
exercises.explain: Plus abstract nouns like Zeit and Hunger, and most place names.
Not an error — a different emphasis. Which is why the rule is „normally no article“ rather than „never“.

exercises.prompt: ___ morgen an gilt der neue Preis.
exercises.explain: von … an marks a starting point in time: from tomorrow onwards.
über for a route via somewhere.
ohne = without, and it always takes the accusative.
über also means „more than“ with a quantity.
ohne + accusative: ohne ein Wort.
sprechen über + Akkusativ — the topic of conversation.
ohne takes the accusative, and neuter is unchanged: ohne mein Auto.

exercises.prompt: ___ jetzt an mache ich mehr Sport.
exercises.explain: von jetzt an — from now on.
ohne belongs to the fixed accusative group: durch, für, gegen, ohne, um.
The starting edge of a period, not its end.
n-Deklination nouns add -n or -en everywhere except the nominative singular.
Nominative singular is the one bare form: der Kunde.
Dative, so the -n appears: dem Kollegen.
Nouns in -ent, -ist, -ent and -oge almost all belong to this group.
der Mensch → den Menschen.
Nominative again, so no ending.
Direct address is the nominative: Herr Müller. But „Ich sehe Herrn Müller“ takes the -n.
Nominative: Ihr Name. („der Name“ is slightly irregular — genitive is des Namens.)

options: -n oder -en in allen Fällen außer Nominativ Singular
exercises.explain: One ending, everywhere but one slot — which is why the nominative is the form to check against.

exercises.prompt: Welches Nomen gehört NICHT zur n-Deklination?
exercises.explain: The group is almost entirely masculine nouns ending in -e, plus -ent/-ist/-ent/-oge. der Tisch is an ordinary masculine noun.
